Grass sways gently in the evening breeze and the mouse leaps from to shadow to shadow across the dimly lit prairie in search of its 
favored meal, the bulbwark. Th ese stone-hard nuts can lay untouched for days as only the lhoupin are able to break their thick shell. 
With a staccato of rapid squeaks, the mouse uses its unique loop ears as a resonating chamber to register the perfect pitch for assessing 
the density of the shell and, with expert accuracy, a nearly imperceptibly high frequency squeak shatters the nut. Although this trait has 
been developed for the procurement of food, when in danger the lhoupin is capable of doing the same against predators, squeaking in 
quick succession to fi gure out the exact pitch necessary to shatter carapace and bone alike.

Encountering Laying low during the daylight hours, the 
lhoupin leave their burrows to forage only after twilight. Often 
roaming alone, their shattering squeak is usually too high a 
pitch to discern, but their questing staccato of squeaks can lead 
a Traveler to the little rodents. Th ough extremely skittish, if one 
fi nds their grassy hole burrows, piling a feast of bulbwark could 
potentially lure them out.

At first glance it may look like a single loop, the 
long hollow ear tips push up against each other 
tightly, allowing sound to vibrate seamlessly 
within, while still separating safely if the loop 
is ever snagged by branch or predator’s claw
Incapable of simply walking, the mouse instead 
hops. Their powerful hind-legs can propel the 
mouse long distances over the relatively flat 
fields and prairies of the Farplains
